source.title: ChemFM as a scaling law guided foundation model pre-trained on informative chemicals
source.authors: Feiyang Cai; Katelin Zacour; Tianyu Zhu; Tzuen-Rong Tzeng; Yongping Duan; Ling Liu; Srikanth Pilla; Gang Li; Feng Luo

record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in chemical language models and reports both a dataset-dependent saturation point and deviations of the 1B and 3B models from the predicted power law.
record.gate_note: The paper tests validation-loss scaling with model size on UniChem and ZINC20, and compares larger ChemFM models with a predicted scaling law. It does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture-shape invariance, or prediction of downstream-task performance from pretraining loss. Downstream benchmark results and comparisons with other models are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits a power law of validation loss against non-embedding parameters for causal chemical language models trained on SMILES, on two datasets. It then checks whether 1B and 3B models fall on the law fitted to the small runs. This is a new setting (molecular strings rather than natural-language text) with its own results on the claim, so T3 fits better than T5. The paper's goal is choosing a pretraining dataset, not refuting scaling laws.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors use the scaling experiments to pick UniChem as the more informative dataset. On UniChem, loss follows a power law in model size (10M–200M) with no saturation. ZINC20 saturates at 60M, which they attribute to the data becoming a bottleneck. The 1B and 3B models' final losses start to deviate from the predicted law, which they read as diminishing returns under the current data regime.
record.recipe_differences: Uses causal decoder-only chemical language models trained on SMILES and validation cross-entropy loss; varies model size with a fixed 250,000-step training budget. It does not test the original text-language-model compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset affects the outcome: UniChem shows a power-law trend in the tested smaller models, while ZINC20 saturates at 60M parameters. On UniChem, final losses for ChemFM-1B and ChemFM-3B deviate from the predicted law.
record.problems: The scaling experiment varies model size but does not independently vary token count or compute, nor test compute-optimal allocations. The text provides no uncertainty estimates for the scaling-law trends or the reported deviations.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant scaling outcomes are reported. Downstream property prediction, generation, reaction prediction, and fine-tuning results do not measure the claim versions about pretraining-loss scaling, compute-optimal allocation, or predictability from pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Natural-language text pretraining is not studied; all results are on SMILES chemical LMs and are recorded under V5.
No fixed-compute sweep and no parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of depth or width at fixed parameter count; model shapes co-vary with size (Table S1.1).
Only model-size scaling at a fixed step budget. No scaling of data or compute, no repeated-data or fine-tuning/transfer scaling laws, and no image or video models.
No test of whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss. Only a 1B-vs-3B comparison and a ZINC20-vs-UniChem pretraining comparison exist.
No comparison of parameter-counting conventions, fitting methods or training schedules as such.
Only two extrapolation points (1B, 3B), with no numerical prediction error reported.

missing.what: Loss trajectories against processed tokens for each model size on both datasets (scaling with tokens at fixed model size could be read from these curves).

Downstream comparison of ChemFM-3B against ChemFM-1B (3B generally better) and of UniChem- against ZINC20-pretrained 1B models, which ties lower-saturation pretraining to better downstream results. Qualitative only, not a predictability test.
missing.locator: Table S2.1; Table S2.6; Results §2.4, Methods §4.13

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 labels were limits_scope; they are changed to supports, because data-dependent saturation and bending away from the fit are what V7 claims. The rows are moved from V1 to V5, since the system is a SMILES chemical LM rather than a text model. The 1B/3B extrapolation check is confounded: those runs used about 818B tokens, one epoch and a cosine schedule, while the fit runs used a fixed 250k steps. No uncertainty or deviation magnitude is reported in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Tests model-size scaling only; does not separately vary training tokens or compute, or test the non-bottleneck condition across those factors.
Tests predictions from the small-model scaling fit for ChemFM-1B and ChemFM-3B only; the text does not report a broader set of extrapolation tests.
No fixed-compute sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is tested.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Tests molecular chemical-language-model pretraining on SMILES, not image or video models, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
Does not test whether downstream performance can be predicted from scale or pretraining loss.
Shows dependence on dataset and deviations at larger model sizes; does not compare parameter-counting conventions, alternative fitting methods, or training schedules.

rows.subject: ChemFM family (ChemFM-10M to ChemFM-200M)
rows.size_stated: approximately 10 million to 200 million parameters; non-embedding parameter counts in Supplementary Fig. S1.1
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and measured validation cross-entropy loss after a fixed 250,000-step data budget.
rows.measure: Validation loss versus non-embedding parameter count
rows.value: Validation loss closely followed a power-law scaling trend with model size, with no sign of performance saturation. Supplementary Fig. S1.1 gives L = (N/433.95)^−0.042.
rows.note: The text reports the trend for the set of models as a whole; the equation is printed in the supplementary figure.
rows.check: SMILES chemical-LM pretraining is a non-text setting, so this belongs under V5 rather than V1. The fitted range is 9.8M–201M non-embedding parameters (Table S1.1), only about 1.3 orders of magnitude, under a fixed 250k-step data budget. The fitted exponent is very small (−0.042). No baseline is needed; the value is correct.

rows.subject: ChemFM family (ChemFM-10M to ChemFM-200M)
rows.size_stated: approximately 10 million to 200 million parameters; model size reached 60 million parameters
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and measured validation cross-entropy loss after a fixed 250,000-step data budget.
rows.value: Performance saturation occurred when model size reached 60M parameters.
rows.note: The authors interpret the saturation as the dataset becoming a bottleneck for further gains from increasing parameter size.
rows.check: Loss follows a decreasing trend up to about 60M parameters, then saturates on ZINC20 (Fig. S1.1d). The authors attribute this to low data diversity (a data bottleneck). Linked to V5 (the form holds only partly) and V7 (the curve bends away from a single power law depending on the data). Not linked to V1, which is about text.

rows.subject: ChemFM-1B
rows.operation_detail: Compared the final validation loss of a large model with the predicted scaling law from smaller models.

conditions.value: predicted scaling law from Supplementary Fig. S1.1

rows.measure: Final validation loss relative to predicted power law
rows.value: The final validation loss starts to deviate from the predicted scaling law.
rows.note: The paper reports the deviation in text but does not provide a numerical deviation for this model there.
rows.check: ChemFM-1B's final loss sits above the small-model fit; the text says 'start to deviate' and gives no number. This is not a clean extrapolation test: the 1B/3B runs were trained for about 818B tokens in one epoch with a cosine schedule. The fit runs used 250k steps (at most about 134B tokens, per Fig. S1.1a). Training tokens and schedule therefore differ from the fitted runs.
